draft.title: Validity, reliability and accuracy
card: is how close a measurement is to the true value. A scale reading 50.0 g for a 50.0 g mass is accurate.
is whether results come out the same, or very close, when the test is repeated. Results can be reliable but not accurate.
is whether a test measures what it aims to measure. A valid test controls the other variables, keeping everything the same except the one being tested.
A result can be reliable and still be off target. A test can have accurate tools but not be valid if it measures the wrong thing or other variables change.
draft.remember: Accurate is close to the true value. Reliable is the same when repeated. Valid is measuring what you meant to, with other variables controlled.

a.q: A student repeats a water temperature test three times and gets 24.1, 24.0 and 24.2 °C. The water is truly 20.0 °C. What describes these results?
a.why: The results are almost the same each time, so they are reliable. They are not close to the true value of 20.0 °C, so they are not accurate.
a.clue: Compare the repeats with each other, then with the true value.

b.q: Sam tests whether fertiliser makes bean plants grow taller. He puts the fertilised plants on a sunny bench and the others on a dark shelf. Why is his test not valid?
opts: Light also differs, so height may not be due to fertiliser
His height measurements are not close to the true value
His repeated results do not come out the same
He used too few types of fertiliser in the investigation
b.why: A valid test controls the other variables, so only the factor being tested changes. Light also changed, so Sam cannot tell whether fertiliser or light caused the difference. Accuracy is about closeness to the true value, which is a different idea.
b.clue: Count how many variables changed between the two groups.

b.best: Light also differs, so height may not be due to fertiliser
